Compassionate

/kum-PAH-shun-it/ — rhymes with 'passionate' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is compassionate feels genuine concern for people who are suffering and wants to help ease their pain.

The compassionate nurse stayed late to comfort the frightened patient.

Worked Example

The nurse stayed late to hold the hand of a patient facing surgery the next morning, listening to their fears without judgment.

Compassionate is precise here because it captures not just kindness, but genuine concern for the patient's suffering combined with a desire to help. The nurse didn't just perform her job; she felt the patient's anxiety and actively eased it. That combination—understanding pain and acting to help—is exactly what compassionate means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

benevolent: Benevolent describes a settled goodwill — wanting good things for people in general, like a benevolent donor funding libraries. Compassionate is more particular and more urgent: it responds to suffering in front of you and moves you to ease it. Benevolence wishes well broadly; compassion answers one person's pain.

sympathetic: Sympathetic means feeling sorry for someone in trouble and showing it — a sympathetic listener nods and says comforting words. Compassionate goes further: the concern turns into action to ease the person's suffering. You can be sympathetic from your chair; being compassionate means doing something about the pain.

humane: Humane means treating people or animals with basic decency and mercy, refusing to cause needless suffering — humane shelters, humane treatment of prisoners. It sets a floor of decent treatment. Compassionate rises above that floor: genuinely feeling another's suffering and wanting to relieve it, not merely declining to add to it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

callous: coldly unfeeling toward other people's suffering

heartless: completely lacking pity or kindness

Where it sits · how deeply someone is moved to help — indifferent → kind → empathetic → compassionate

indifferent vs. compassionate: Indifferent sits at the opposite end of the scale from compassionate: an indifferent person simply does not care about others' suffering, while a compassionate person is deeply moved to help.

kind vs. compassionate: Kind is weaker than compassionate: a kind person is pleasant and caring in ordinary ways, while a compassionate person feels genuine concern for someone's suffering and wants to ease it.

empathetic vs. compassionate: Empathetic comes close to compassionate but stops one step short: an empathetic person feels another's pain as if it were their own, while a compassionate person also feels driven to relieve it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — com-

Prefix — com-: with, together (Latin)

Root — pass

Root — pass: to suffer (from Latin pati, 'to suffer'; its past form gives pass-)

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: act or state of (Latin)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: having the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Com- ('with') + pass ('to suffer,' from Latin pati) + -ion ('state of') + -ate ('having the quality of') builds the literal meaning 'suffering with someone' — exactly what a compassionate person does: they feel another person's pain alongside them and want to ease it.

Use the root in a new word: patient

Use the root in a new word: patient: A hospital patient is literally 'one who suffers' — the same Latin root pati ('to suffer') that makes a compassionate person someone who suffers with others.
